title: Median and mode
summary: How to find the median for an odd and an even number of observations, why the median is preferred with extreme values, and the mode with bimodal and multimodal data.

chunks.heading: Median: the middle value
chunks.explanation_md:
The **median** of a data set is the **value in the middle** when the data items are **arranged in ascending order**. Ordering first is not optional: no sorting, no median.

Why bother with it when we have the mean? The slide's answer:

- **Whenever a data set has extreme values, the median is the preferred measure of central location.**
- The median is the measure of location **most often reported for annual income and property value data**. The professor adds a bold **(Not always)** here, so do not write that it is always used.
- The reason: **a few extremely large incomes or property values can inflate the mean.** The median does not get pulled up the same way.

key_terms.meaning: The value in the middle when the data items are arranged in ascending order.

chunks.exam_line: With extreme values the median is the preferred measure of central location; a few extremely large incomes or property values can inflate the mean.

chunks.heading: Odd number of observations
chunks.explanation_md:
The slide's data: **26, 18, 27, 12, 14, 27, 19** (7 observations).

**Step 1: arrange in ascending order.** 12, 14, 18, 19, 26, 27, 27

**Step 2: find the middle position.**

Median = ((n + 1)/2)th term

With n = 7: (7 + 1)/2 = 4, so the 4th term.

**Step 3: read it off.** The 4th term is **19**.

**Median = 19.** Three values sit below it (12, 14, 18) and three above (26, 27, 27).
chunks.exam_line: Odd n: arrange in ascending order, Median = ((n + 1)/2)th term. For 26, 18, 27, 12, 14, 27, 19 the median is 19.

check_questions.stem: For an odd number of observations, Median = ((n + 1)/____)th term.
With 7 observations in ascending order, which term is the median?
options: The average of the 3rd and 4th terms

chunks.heading: Even number of observations
chunks.explanation_md:
Add one value, 30, and you get **26, 18, 27, 12, 14, 27, 30, 19** (8 observations).

**Step 1: arrange in ascending order.** 12, 14, 18, 19, 26, 27, 27, 30

**Step 2: there is no single middle value**, so the median is the **average of the middle two values**:

Median = ((n/2)th term + (n/2 + 1)th term) / 2

With n = 8: the 4th term and the 5th term, which are **19** and **26**.

**Step 3: average them.**

Median = (19 + 26)/2 = **22.5**

Notice that 22.5 is not one of the eight data values.
chunks.exam_line: Even n: Median = ((n/2)th term + (n/2 + 1)th term)/2. For the slide's 8 values: (19 + 26)/2 = 22.5.

check_questions.stem: With 8 observations in ascending order, the median is the average of which terms?
For an even number of observations, the median is the average of the middle two values.

chunks.heading: Mode: the most frequent value
chunks.explanation_md:
The **mode** of a data set is the **value that occurs with the greatest frequency**.

Three rules from the slide:

- The greatest frequency **can occur at two or more different values**.
- If the data have **exactly two modes**, the data are **bimodal**.
- If the data have **more than two modes**, the data are **multimodal**.

Quick try with the odd-numbered median data: 26, 18, 27, 12, 14, **27**, 19. Only 27 appears twice, so the **mode is 27**.

key_terms.meaning: The value that occurs with the greatest frequency.
Data with more than two modes.

chunks.exam_line: Mode = value with the greatest frequency; exactly two modes = bimodal; more than two modes = multimodal.

chunks.heading: Class Height Exercise: median and mode rounds
chunks.explanation_md:
The **Class Height Exercise** comes back twice:

- after the median slides, the activity asks for the **Median** of the class heights;
- after the mode slide, it asks for the **Mode**.

No heights are printed on the slides. The method you need is the one above:

- **Median**: arrange the heights in **ascending order**, then take the **middle value** (odd count) or the **average of the middle two values** (even count).
- **Mode**: the height that occurs with the **greatest frequency**. If two heights tie, the data are bimodal; more than two, multimodal.
chunks.exam_line: Median: sort first, then middle value or average of the middle two. Mode: the value with the greatest frequency.

questions.stem: Differentiate between the median and the mode.
questions.model_answer_md:
Both are measures of central tendency, but they find the centre differently.

| Basis | Median | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| **Meaning** | **Middle value** when data are in ascending order | Value that occurs with the **greatest frequency** |
| **How many** | Always one | Can be **two (bimodal)**, **more (multimodal)** or **none** |
| **Slide example** | 26, 18, 27, 12, 14, 27, 19 gives 19 | The same data give 27 |
| **Data type** | Ordinal and numerical data | The **only way to represent nominal data** |

Both are **not affected by extreme values**.

rubric.point: Median: middle value after sorting
Mode: greatest frequency; can be bimodal, multimodal or none
Example values 19 and 27
Mode is the only measure for nominal data; both resist extreme values

questions.stem: As the manager of the 15 retail stores, find the median and the mode(s) of monthly sales and interpret them.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Sorted sales (₹ lakhs):** 27, 28, 29, 30, 30, 31, 32, 34, 34, 35, 36, 38, 39, 41, 44 (n = 15).

**Median:** n is odd, so Median = ((n + 1)/2)th term = (16/2) = 8th term = **34**. Half the stores sell ₹34 lakhs or less, half ₹34 lakhs or more.

**Mode:** 30 (stores 10 and 15) and 34 (stores 2 and 9) each appear twice. Two modes, so the sales are **bimodal**.

**Interpretation:** the slide asks you to find clusters of stores at a figure and study what they share (location, management style, product mix). Here there are **two small clusters**, at 30 and at 34, not one.

rubric.point: Sort and use the 8th term: median 34
Modes 30 and 34: bimodal
Clusters: stores 10 and 15 at 30; stores 2 and 9 at 34
Link to studying common features of clustered stores

questions.stem: Explain the median: its definition, how to find it for an odd and an even number of observations (with the slide's examples) and when it is the preferred measure of central location.
questions.model_answer_md:
The **median** is the value in the **middle** when the data are **arranged in ascending order**. It separates the data into a higher and a lower half.

**Step 1 every time: sort the data.**

**Odd number of observations**
- Formula: **Median = ((n + 1)/2)th term**.
- Slide data: 26, 18, 27, 12, 14, 27, 19 (n = 7).
- Sorted: 12, 14, 18, **19**, 26, 27, 27.
- (7 + 1)/2 = 4th term, so **Median = 19**.

**Even number of observations**
- Formula: **Median = ((n/2)th term + (n/2 + 1)th term) / 2**, the average of the middle two values.
- Slide data: 26, 18, 27, 12, 14, 27, 30, 19 (n = 8).
- Sorted: 12, 14, 18, **19, 26**, 27, 27, 30.
- 4th and 5th terms: **Median = (19 + 26)/2 = 22.5**, which is not itself a data value.

**When the median is preferred**
- **Whenever a data set has extreme values**, the median is the preferred measure of central location.
- It is the measure **most often reported for annual income and property value data** (the professor marks this **not always**).
- Reason: **a few extremely large incomes or property values can inflate the mean**; the median stays with the typical value.

**In class:** the **Class Height Exercise** returns for a median round, using the same method on the class's heights.

**Conclusion:** sort, find the middle (one value or the average of two), and prefer the median when extreme values are present.

rubric.point: Definition: middle value after arranging in ascending order
Odd n: ((n + 1)/2)th term; example gives 19
Even n: average of (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th terms; example gives 22.5
Preferred when data have extreme values
Income and property data (not always); large values inflate the mean

questions.stem: Define the mode and explain the terms bimodal and multimodal. Find the mode of each of these slide data sets and comment: (a) 26, 18, 27, 12, 14, 27, 19; (b) Supplier-1; (c) Player-1's runs; (d) the 15 retail stores' sales.
questions.model_answer_md:
The **mode** of a data set is the **value that occurs with the greatest frequency**.

**Rules from the slide:**
- The greatest frequency **can occur at two or more different values**.
- **Exactly two modes:** the data are **bimodal**.
- **More than two modes:** the data are **multimodal**.

**Finding the modes**

**(a) 26, 18, 27, 12, 14, 27, 19:** only 27 appears twice. **Mode = 27.**

**(b) Supplier-1 (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11):** only 6 appears twice. **Mode = 6**, the same as its mean and median.

**(c) Player-1 (78, 2, 67, 45, 8, 0, 4, 78, 90, 3, 12, 12, 56, 3, 4, 5, 90, 90, 4, 4):** 4 appears four times, 90 three times. **Mode = 4.** So Player-1's most common score is very low, even though the mean is much higher.

**(d) 15 retail stores:** 30 and 34 each appear twice, every other value once. **Modes = 30 and 34**, so the data are **bimodal**.

**Comment:**
- The mode shows the **most typical or most popular** value, which is why it guides choices like the most sold t-shirt size.
- It can give **more than one answer**, as in (d), and a manager should not ignore multiple modes when they matter for planning.
- It is **not affected by extreme values**: Player-1's 90s do not change the mode of 4.

**Conclusion:** count frequencies, pick the most frequent value, and report every mode if there is more than one.

rubric.point: Mode: value with the greatest frequency
Bimodal: exactly two modes; multimodal: more than two
(c) Player-1 mode 4
(d) 30 and 34: bimodal
Mode not affected by extreme values; can have several values
